t.6.39.1: Bound by the dreadful binding of arrows, the two sons of Daśaratha lay drenched in blood, breathing heavily like a pair of serpents.
t.6.39.2: All those foremost of the vānaras, mighty in strength, together with Sugrīva, surrounded the two great-souled ones and stood there, overwhelmed with grief.
t.6.39.3: Meanwhile the valiant Rāma regained consciousness, owing to his steadfastness and the strength of his spirit, even though he was bound fast by the arrows.
t.6.39.5: What use is Sītā to me now, or what use is life itself, to me who today see my brother lying vanquished in battle?
t.6.39.4: Then, seeing his brother covered in blood, despondent, deeply pierced, and with a woeful face, he lamented in anguish.
t.6.39.6: By one who searches through the world, a woman equal to Sītā can be found, but not a brother equal to Lakṣmaṇa, a counselor and companion in battle.
t.6.39.7: If the one who increases Sumitrā's joy has gone to his death, I shall give up my life while the monkeys look on.
t.6.39.8: What shall I say to my mother Kausalyā, and what to Kaikayī? And how shall I speak to mother Sumitrā, who longs to see her son?
t.6.39.9: How shall I console her, bereft of her son, trembling and crying out like a female osprey, if I go back without him?
t.6.39.10: How shall I speak to Śatrughna and to the illustrious Bharata, saying, "He went to the forest together with me, and I have come back again without him"?
t.6.39.12: Shame on me, ignoble and a doer of evil deeds, on whose account this Lakṣmaṇa lies fallen on a bed of arrows like one whose life has departed!
t.6.39.11: Alas, I shall not be able to bear the reproach made by Sumitrā. Here itself I shall abandon my body, for I cannot bear to live.
t.6.39.13: O Lakṣmaṇa, you always used to console me when I was deeply dejected; but today, your life departed, you cannot speak to me in my distress.
t.6.39.14: He by whom many Rākṣasas were struck down to the earth in battle today, that hero now lies on that very earth, struck down by his foes.
t.6.39.15: Lying on this bed of arrows, drenched in his own blood and covered with masses of arrows, he shines like the sun going to its setting.
t.6.39.17: Just as that greatly splendid one followed me when I was going to the forest, so too shall I follow him to the abode of Yama.
t.6.39.16: Because his vital parts have been struck by arrows, he cannot look about; and though he does not speak, the redness of his eyes shows that he is in pain.
t.6.39.19: I do not recall that the heroic Lakṣmaṇa, even when greatly enraged, ever made me hear anything harsh or unpleasant.
t.6.39.18: He who always cherished his kinsfolk and was ever devoted to me has today come to this state through the misdeeds of ignoble me.
t.6.39.20: Lakṣmaṇa is superior in arrows and missiles even to Kārtavīrya, who loosed five hundred arrows in a single burst.
t.6.39.21: He who could strike down with his weapons the weapons even of great-souled Śakra, that same one, accustomed to a costly bed, now lies slain upon the earth.
t.6.39.22: And that falsely spoken word of mine will surely burn me, there is no doubt, since Vibhīṣaṇa has not been made king of the rākṣasas by me.
t.6.39.24: Placing Aṅgada at the front, O Sugrīva, cross the ocean again by that very bridge, together with your army and your band of friends.
t.6.39.23: At this very moment, Sugrīva, you should go back from here, O king, for the mighty Rāvaṇa, thinking you deprived of me, may rush upon you.
t.6.39.26: Great deeds were done by Aṅgada, by Mainda and by Dvivida; in the battle a terrible fight was fought by Kesarin and by Sampāti.
t.6.39.25: Hanumān has accomplished a deed in battle that would be hard for others to perform. I am pleased with the king of the bears and with the lord of the cow-tailed monkeys as well.
t.6.39.28: Fate cannot be overcome by mortal men, O Sugrīva; but whatever could be done by a companion or a friend, O scorcher of foes, all that has been done by you, O Sugrīva, who fear unrighteousness.
t.6.39.27: For my sake a battle was fought by Gavaya, Gavākṣa, Śarabha and Gaja, and by other monkeys who had abandoned all care for their lives.
t.6.39.29: O bulls among the monkeys, you have accomplished this task of friendship. Having been granted leave by me, all of you may go wherever you wish.
t.6.39.31: Then Vibhīṣaṇa, having stationed all the troops, came in haste, mace in hand, to where Rāghava was.
t.6.39.30: All those monkeys heard his lamentation, and they, whose eyes were not dark but tawny, shed tears from their eyes.
t.6.39.32: Seeing him moving swiftly, resembling a heap of dark collyrium, all the vānaras fled, taking him to be Rāvaṇi.
